t: Source Code Structure Extractor: a plain-language overview
title: Source Code Structure Extractor: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Source Code Structure Extractor does and why archives need it. A source code structure extractor reads a program file the way a compiler does and writes down what it finds: every function, every class, every import, and how they connect. It does not run the code; it studies its shape. The result is a structured map of the program that search engines and archives can index.
demo:
# Source Code Structure Extractor - runnable demo (JAH-ATK151-000001)
import ast
RANK = 1
SIG = False
SAMPLE = "def greet(name):\n    return 'hi ' + name\n\nclass Bot:\n    def reply(self, msg):\n        return greet(msg)\n\nimport json\nprint(json.dumps(greet('sam')))"
tree = ast.parse(SAMPLE)
funcs = [(n.name, n.lineno) for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef)]
classes = [(n.name, n.lineno) for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.ClassDef)]
imports = [n.names[0].name for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Import)]
calls = sorted({n.func.id for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Name)})
print("functions:", funcs)
print("classes:", classes)
print("imports:", imports)
if RANK >= 2:
    print("call sites:", calls)
if RANK >= 3:
    print("defined names:", sorted({n for n, _ in funcs} | {n for n, _ in classes}))
    print("external calls:", [c for c in calls if c not in {n for n, _ in funcs}])
if SIG:
    print("Signature lineage stamp: JAH-SIG-STRUCT-" + "JAH-ATK151-000001")
print("record:", "JAH-ATK151-000001", "OK")
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Source Code Structure Extractor works: the deep tour
title: How the Source Code Structure Extractor works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Source Code Structure Extractor does and why archives need it. Real extractors parse source text into an abstract syntax tree (AST) with tools like Python's ast module, tree-sitter, or Roslyn, then walk the tree recording definitions: functions, classes, modules, variables, imports, decorators, and annotations. Concrete syntax trees keep every token including comments, while symbol tables resolve names to their definitions. From the tree the extractor emits structured records — name, kind, location, signature, docstring — that make code searchable without running it. Production extractors handle many languages through one grammar framework (tree-sitter ships parsers for dozens of languages), recover gracefully from syntax errors in partial files, and resolve cross-file references by following import statements. Quality is measured by definition recall on annotated corpora and by round-trip fidelity: the tree must regenerate the original source. Limits appear with macros, eval-style dynamic code, and generated sources, where static structure understates what the program actually does.

Real extractors parse source text into an abstract syntax tree (AST) with tools like Python's ast module, tree-sitter, or Roslyn, then walk the tree recording definitions: functions, classes, modules, variables, imports, decorators, and annotations. Concrete syntax trees keep every token including comments, while symbol tables resolve names to their definitions. From the tree the extractor emits structured records — name, kind, location, signature, docstring — that make code searchable without running it.
demo:
# Source Code Structure Extractor - runnable demo (JAH-ATK151-000014)
import ast
RANK = 2
SIG = False
SAMPLE = "import os\ndef scan(path):\n    return [f for f in os.listdir(path)]\n\ndef main():\n    files = scan('.')\n    print(len(files))"
tree = ast.parse(SAMPLE)
funcs = [(n.name, n.lineno) for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef)]
classes = [(n.name, n.lineno) for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.ClassDef)]
imports = [n.names[0].name for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Import)]
calls = sorted({n.func.id for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Name)})
print("functions:", funcs)
print("classes:", classes)
print("imports:", imports)
if RANK >= 2:
    print("call sites:", calls)
if RANK >= 3:
    print("defined names:", sorted({n for n, _ in funcs} | {n for n, _ in classes}))
    print("external calls:", [c for c in calls if c not in {n for n, _ in funcs}])
if SIG:
    print("Signature lineage stamp: JAH-SIG-STRUCT-" + "JAH-ATK151-000014")
print("record:", "JAH-ATK151-000014", "OK")

title: The Source Code Structure Extractor at archive scale
description: Production: how the Source Code Structure Extractor runs at archive scale and plugs into the extraction pipeline. Real extractors parse source text into an abstract syntax tree (AST) with tools like Python's ast module, tree-sitter, or Roslyn, then walk the tree recording definitions: functions, classes, modules, variables, imports, decorators, and annotations. Concrete syntax trees keep every token including comments, while symbol tables resolve names to their definitions. From the tree the extractor emits structured records — name, kind, location, signature, docstring — that make code searchable without running it. Production extractors handle many languages through one grammar framework (tree-sitter ships parsers for dozens of languages), recover gracefully from syntax errors in partial files, and resolve cross-file references by following import statements. Quality is measured by definition recall on annotated corpora and by round-trip fidelity: the tree must regenerate the original source. Limits appear with macros, eval-style dynamic code, and generated sources, where static structure understates what the program actually does.
